title: The staff and the shining hand
word: The staff and the shining hand
hook: his staff becomes a snake and his hand comes out white and shining: two signs

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kalimullah, called from the fire on the mountain and told to take off his sandals. Your line was you are in a sacred valley. Today, the end of the week.

Look down at your hands. What's in them? A phone, probably. A coffee. A steering wheel, hopefully not. It's easy to stop noticing what you carry. Musa is still standing barefoot in the sacred valley. He's just been told who God is, and that he's been chosen. The next thing he hears isn't a thunderclap or a list of orders. It's a question, almost casual, the kind a friend asks, about the thing in his hand.
screen: `WHAT'S IN YOUR HANDS?` → `STILL BAREFOOT IN THE VALLEY.` → `A QUESTION, NOT AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha. In Pickthall's old translation: "And what is that in thy right hand, O Moses?" Of course Allah knows what it is. So why ask? Some commentators say it was to make Musa look closely at something ordinary, so he'd know exactly what it was before it changed. And Musa answers at length. It's my staff. I lean on it. I knock leaves down with it for my sheep. And I have other uses for it too. Some commentators smile at that long answer: a man just spoken to by his Lord, who doesn't want the conversation to end. Then: throw it down. He does, and it's a snake, moving fast. Take it, and don't be afraid; We'll return it to how it was. Then the second sign: put your hand under your arm, and it will come out white, without any harm. The Qur'an adds that phrase, and commentators read it as ruling out illness: light, not sickness. Two signs, both from what he already has. A shepherd's stick. His own hand. Nothing brought down from the sky. The ordinary thing, looked at properly, turns out to be enough for the mission. And that's the week. A mother's hands letting go of a chest. A queen's arms. A sister who spoke up. A blow Musa regretted. Water at a well. A fire on a mountain. And now a staff. Seven days, and most of the turning points were in someone's hands.
screen: `WHAT IS THAT IN THY RIGHT HAND?` · `MY STAFF: I LEAN ON IT.` · `A SNAKE, THEN A STAFF AGAIN.` · `A HAND, SHINING, WITHOUT HARM.` · then, large: `TWO SIGNS, FROM WHAT HE HAD.`

segments.voice: Look at what's in your hand, the phone or the cup, or your empty hand: turn it over, see the lines, the knuckles, the small scar you forgot you had. Then ask the question the way it was asked in the valley, what is this, and answer honestly, at length if you like, like Musa: what does it do for you, and what else could it be used for? If you pray, you can offer what's in your hand to Allah.
The staff and the shining hand: two signs, made from a shepherd's stick and his own hand.
screen: `THE STAFF AND THE SHINING HAND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what's in your right hand? Usually, something ordinary. A week with Musa, done.

howItsDone: Muslims count the staff and the shining hand among the signs, ayat, given to Musa, and the story is often told to show how Allah works through ordinary things.

original.note: Arabic: staff, the shepherd's stick Musa leaned on, from Qur'an 20:18.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic trick with a stick.
what it means: two signs, the staff and the shining hand, both made from what Musa already had, given before he goes to Pharaoh.
what a scholar hears: 20:22 adds min ghayri su', "without any harm," so the white hand is not read as disease; commentators say the question in 20:17 was to make him look closely first.

sources.quoted: And what is that in thy right hand, O Moses?

notes: Quotation of 20:17 from Pickthall 1930 given from memory; please verify the exact wording against the 1930 text.
Commentary points (why Allah asks; Musa's long answer out of love of the conversation) stated as 'many/some commentators say'. Confirm.
'Put your hand under your arm' paraphrases 20:22 (idmum yadaka ila janahika), often rendered 'to your side'. Confirm.
